kf1.tip: Sketch from memory the route blood takes from the vena cava to the aorta, labelling all four chambers and marking where the blood picks up oxygen.
kf1.note: A good sketch runs vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium, left ventricle, aorta. Check you labelled both atria and both ventricles, and marked the lungs as where blood picks up oxygen. Everything before the lungs is deoxygenated and on the right side. Everything after is oxygenated and on the left. If you sent blood from an atrium straight into an artery, you skipped a ventricle.

kf2.tip: Rank stents, statins, heart transplants and artificial hearts from best to worst for a patient with early coronary heart disease, and defend each place in one line.
kf2.note: A strong answer weighs how severe the disease is, how risky each treatment is, and how long it lasts. Most would put statins first, since early disease means slowing fatty build-up, though they are long-term and can cause headaches and muscle pain. Stents come next: effective, but with infection and clot risks. Transplants and artificial hearts sit last because they are for severe cases. The trap is ranking a transplant top because it replaces the whole heart.

cs1.tip: Write the chain from atheroma building up in the coronary arteries to a heart attack, then mark the link a stent breaks and the link statins break.
cs1.note: A good chain runs: fatty atheroma builds up, the coronary artery narrows, less blood flows to the heart muscle, the muscle gets too little oxygen, heart attack. A stent breaks the link between narrowing and reduced blood flow, because it holds the artery open. Statins act earlier, at the build-up itself, by lowering blood cholesterol and slowing fatty deposits. If you said statins clear the blockage, check again: they slow the build-up.
